Reproducing Sohn et al. (2019) from dandiset 000130¶

Paper. Sohn H, Narain D, Meirhaeghe N, Jazayeri M (2019). Bayesian computation through cortical latent dynamics. Neuron 103(5):934-947. doi:10.1016/j.neuron.2019.06.012. This attempt used the full text of the accepted author manuscript in PubMed Central (PMC6805134). The supplementary figures and tables (Tables S1 to S3) were not available to it.

Dandiset. DANDI:000130, version 0.241017.1448. The paper cites no DANDI version (it predates the dandiset, which was made for the Neural Latents Benchmark in 2021). Of the two published versions, 0.220113.0407 and 0.241017.1448, this is the most recent. Both hold the same two files (same asset and blob ids and sizes), and their metadata differ only in the publication date, the citation and the repository URL's trailing slash, so neither matches the paper better.

What the dandiset holds. One recording session (2016-12-11) of monkey H ("Haydn"), from the Neural Latents Benchmark (NLB): a train file with the full trial table and the spikes of 54 units, and a test file with 283 further trials of the same session that carry no task variables and only 40 of the units. The paper analyses 17 sessions of monkey H and 12 of monkey G. Monkey G is not in the dandiset. All results here come from this one session, and a "dataset" is one effector and target direction (4 here; the paper's 8 are 2 animals x 4).

Code. The paper's code is "available from the corresponding author on request" and was not read. The dandiset links the NLB, whose code (nlb_tools at commit 42f8410b) loads these files, builds tensors aligned to Go (1500 ms before Go), and scores models by a trial-by-trial correlation of neural speed with tp within each prior, effector and direction. It holds none of the paper's analyses; its speed measure (mean step between successive states) matches the one chosen here.

Column descriptions (train trial table):
   start_time: Start time of epoch, in seconds
   stop_time: Stop time of epoch, in seconds
   fix_on_time: Time when the fixation cue on the display turns on
   fix_time: Time when the animal fixates on the fixation cue
   target_on_time: Time of target presentation
   ready_time: Time of ready cue delivery
   set_time: Time of set cue presentation
   go_time: Time of monkey response, either with an eye saccade or joystick movement
   target_acq_time: Time of target acquisition
   reward_time: Time of monkey reward, if there was one
   bad_time: Time of trial failure, if the trial was unsuccessful
   is_short: Whether short prior (True) or long prior (False)
   is_eye: Whether motion to target was with hand (False) or eye (True)
   theta: Whether the target was on the right (0) or left (180)
   ts: Time between ready and set stimuli, in ms
   tp: Time between set stimulus and monkey go response, in ms
   fix_time_dur: Time between animal fixation and target onset, in ms
   target_time_dur: Time between target onset and ready, in ms
   iti: Inter-trial interval, in ms. Equal to 500 for trials sampled from short prior and 1220 for trials sampled from long prior
   reward_dur: Duration of reward, in ms
   is_outlier: Whether a trial's tp is considered an outlier using probabilistic mixture model
   split: Trial split that the trial belongs to for the Neural Latents Benchmark. Can be "train", "val", "test", or "none"

The dandiset summary says one subject (Rhesus monkey) and 2 files, which the files confirm. The test file holds 283 trials of the same session (session_id 20161211) with only start_time, stop_time, go_time and split, on its own clock (0 to 509 s), and only the 40 held-in units; its task variables and the 14 held-out units are withheld for the benchmark. These trials cannot enter any analysis that needs ts, the prior or the effector, so the analyses use the train file's trials. Each condition has at least 14 used trials, so the Methods' rule of at least 5 trials per condition does not remove any unit.

# Refit of the Methods' mixture model, per prior, ts, effector and direction, on completed trials.
flags = []
for key, g in c[c.tp > 0].groupby(["is_short", "ts", "is_eye", "theta"]):
    r = rsg.outlier_mixture(g.tp.to_numpy(), key[1])
    flags.append(pd.Series(r > 0.5, index=g.index))
refit = pd.concat(flags).reindex(c.index, fill_value=True)
print("\nMixture-model refit against is_outlier (completed trials):")
print(pd.crosstab(c.is_outlier.rename("is_outlier"), refit.rename("refit lapse")).to_string())
print(f"Outlier fraction of completed trials: file {c.is_outlier.mean():.2%}, refit {refit.mean():.2%}; paper, monkey H: 3.84%")
only_file = c[c.is_outlier & ~refit]
print("tp / ts of trials flagged by the file but kept by the refit: %.2f to %.2f (%d trials); of trials flagged by both: %s"
      % ((only_file.tp / only_file.ts).min(), (only_file.tp / only_file.ts).max(), len(only_file),
         np.round(np.sort((c[c.is_outlier & refit].tp / c[c.is_outlier & refit].ts).to_numpy()), 2).tolist()))

ts is the nominal interval; the event times give intervals within 23.5 ms of it, consistent with a 60 Hz display (one frame is 16.7 ms). tp is a median 18 ms longer than go_time - set_time for used trials, so the two columns do not measure the same interval; the analyses use tp for behaviour, as the trial table defines it, and the event times for aligning spikes. The iti values agree with the paper (1220 ms after Short trials, 500 ms after Long ones), and its column description (500 for Short, 1220 for Long) has them the other way round. The is_outlier flag marks 46 completed trials (4.47%, against 3.84% for monkey H in the paper). A refit of the Methods' mixture model as read here, per prior, ts, effector and direction, flags only 10 of them and no other trial; the 36 others have tp between the ratios to ts printed above, which the refit keeps as part of the Gaussian component. How the flag was computed is not documented beyond "probabilistic mixture model". The analyses use the file's flag, as the claims file fixes.

# Recordings deposited twice: does any test trial reappear in the train file? Compare the
# inter-spike-interval sequence of each test trial with the whole train recording, for 3 units.
hits, checked = 0, 0
for uid in T["unit_ids"][:3]:
    s_tr = np.round(np.diff(spikes[int(np.flatnonzero(S["unit_ids"] == uid)[0])]), 4)
    s_te = T["spikes"][int(np.flatnonzero(T["unit_ids"] == uid)[0])]
    for a, b in zip(T["trials"].start_time, T["trials"].stop_time):
        pat = np.round(np.diff(s_te[(s_te >= a) & (s_te < b)]), 4)
        if len(pat) < 3:
            continue
        checked += 1
        hits += any(np.array_equal(s_tr[i:i + len(pat)], pat) for i in np.flatnonzero(s_tr == pat[0]))
print(f"\nTest trials whose spike pattern recurs in the train file: {hits} of {checked} checked (3 units)")
seg = rsg.counts(spikes, units, good.ready_time.to_numpy(), 0, 400, 400)[:, 0, :]
dup = pd.DataFrame(seg).duplicated().sum()
print("Train trials with identical spike counts in all kept units over Ready to Ready + 400 ms:", int(dup))

The 48 units kept by the Methods' rate rule match the paper's count for the single session of monkey H used for GPFA (Methods, N = 48), which is consistent with this being that session; the dandiset does not say so. All units share six observation intervals separated by gaps of 0.1 to 0.14 s; every trial lies inside one interval. No test trial repeats a stretch of the train file, and no two train trials are identical, so no recording is deposited twice. The units carry no single-unit or multi-unit label, no electrode, and the electrode table has no positions or impedances.

# Do spikes share the clock of the trial table? Decode "before" against "after" an event from the
# population counts in 200 ms windows, with the event time shifted by an offset. A response
# locked to the event gives the best decoding at zero offset.
rng_clock = np.random.default_rng(1)
offsets = [-400, -200, -100, -50, 0, 50, 100, 200, 400]
rows = []
for event in ["ready_time", "set_time", "go_time"]:
    for off in offsets:
        t0 = good[event].to_numpy() + off / 1000
        pre = rsg.counts(spikes, units, t0, -200, 0, 200)[:, 0, :]
        post = rsg.counts(spikes, units, t0, 0, 200, 200)[:, 0, :]
        X = np.sqrt(np.vstack([pre, post]))
        y = np.r_[np.zeros(len(pre)), np.ones(len(post))]
        perm = rng_clock.permutation(len(y))
        acc = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000), X[perm], y[perm], cv=5).mean()
        rows.append({"event": event, "offset_ms": off, "accuracy": acc})
clock = pd.DataFrame(rows).pivot(index="offset_ms", columns="event", values="accuracy")
print("Cross-validated accuracy, before against after the event (chance 0.5):")
print(clock.round(3).to_string())
print("Offset of best decoding:", clock.idxmax().to_dict())

# Contrast between conditions: decode the prior from the counts in the 400 ms before Ready, with
# the trial labels as they are and shifted by one block of trials.
pre_ready = np.sqrt(rsg.counts(spikes, units, good.ready_time.to_numpy(), -400, 0, 400)[:, 0, :])
for shift in [0, 25, 50]:
    y = np.roll(good.is_short.to_numpy(), shift)
    perm = rng_clock.permutation(len(y))
    acc = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000), pre_ready[perm], y[perm], cv=5).mean()
    print(f"Prior decoded before Ready, labels shifted by {shift} trials: accuracy {acc:.3f}")

Decoding of "before against after" is best at an offset of +100 ms for Ready, Set and Go, and falls for negative offsets (at -400 ms, 0.56, 0.68 and 0.73). A best offset of +100 ms is what a response with a latency of about 100 ms after each event gives, since the "after" window then holds the response. The prior is decoded from the 400 ms before Ready with accuracy 0.64 with the labels in place, 0.56 and 0.52 with the labels shifted by 25 and 50 trials. This is consistent with the spikes and the trial table sharing one clock in the train file; it does not prove it. The test file could not be checked this way, as it has no task variables; it is not used.

Behaviour¶

beh-slopes¶

Regression slopes of tp on ts are positive and less than one in every condition, so the animals estimated ts and their responses were biased toward the mean of the prior (Figure 1E).

Result: not reproduced. Six of the 8 slopes lie between 0 and 1 (0.50 to 0.90), and 5 of 8 have 95% intervals that exclude both 0 and 1. In the Short prior with the eye, the slopes are 1.11 (Eye Right, interval 1.01 to 1.21) and 1.01 (Eye Left), so in these two conditions this session shows no regression toward the mean. All slopes are positive. The criterion needs all 8 between 0 and 1. The paper's slopes pool 17 sessions of monkey H and 12 of G; this is one session.

beh-overlap-prior¶

At the overlapping ts of 800 ms, biases were in opposite directions for the two priors (rank-sum test, p < 1e-43 in animal H over 17 sessions).

Result: not reproduced. At ts = 800 ms the median bias is +28.3 ms in the Short prior and +47.6 ms in the Long prior, so both are positive and not of opposite sign; the rank-sum test gives p = 0.073 (93 and 107 trials). The Long prior gives the longer tp in 2 of 4 datasets, Hand Right (+29.7 against +96.8 ms, p = 0.00099) and Hand Left (-61.6 against -2.8 ms, p = 0.069), where the Short bias is negative. In the eye datasets the Short tp is the longer (Eye Left +79.1 against +18.6 ms, p = 0.051).

beh-bayes-model¶

A Bayesian observer model with scalar measurement and production noise fit to the behaviour captures the bias and the variance of tp in all conditions (Figure 2C and 2D).

In [11]:
models, rows, pred_rows = {}, [], []
for e, th, name in DS:
    g = good[(good.is_eye == e) & (good.theta == th)]
    m = rsg.BayesObserver.fit(g)
    models[name] = m
    obs_bias, pred_bias, obs_sd, pred_sd = [], [], [], []
    for short in [True, False]:
        ts = np.array(rsg.prior_ts(short), float)
        _, mean_tp, sd_tp = m.moments(ts, short)
        gg = g[g.is_short == short].groupby("ts").tp.agg(["mean", "std"]).loc[ts]
        obs_bias += list(gg["mean"] - ts)
        pred_bias += list(mean_tp - ts)
        obs_sd += list(gg["std"])
        pred_sd += list(sd_tp)
        for t, ob, pb, os_, ps in zip(ts, gg["mean"] - ts, mean_tp - ts, gg["std"], sd_tp):
            pred_rows.append({"dataset": name, "prior": "Short" if short else "Long", "ts": t,
                              "bias_obs": ob, "bias_model": pb, "sd_obs": os_, "sd_model": ps})
    ob, pb = np.array(obs_bias), np.array(pred_bias)
    r2 = 1 - np.sum((ob - pb) ** 2) / np.sum((ob - ob.mean()) ** 2)
    r_sd = stats.pearsonr(obs_sd, pred_sd)[0]
    rows.append({"dataset": name, "wm": m.wm, "wp": m.wp, "b_short": m.b[True], "b_long": m.b[False],
                 "converged": m.converged, "bias_R2": r2, "sd_r": r_sd})

Result: partially reproduced. The observer model predicts the SD of tp with a positive correlation in all 4 datasets (r = 0.28 to 0.91), but its predicted bias reaches R2 >= 0.8 in only 2 of 4 (R2 = 0.12, 0.67, 0.87 and 0.98). The two eye datasets, whose Short slopes exceed 1 (beh-slopes), get very low measurement noise (wm = 0.013 and 0.025) and are the poorly fit ones. Every fit converged. Table S3 was not available, so the fitted parameters are not compared with the paper's.

Single units¶

glm-prior-ts¶

About 30% of neurons were modulated by elapsed time (27% in monkey H) and more than 60% were sensitive to the prior (65% in monkey H) (Figure 3E).

In [13]:
def glm_rows(trs, ts_values):
    # One row per trial and time point t (ms after Ready) for which Set came after t (attrition).
    elapsed = ((trs.set_time - trs.ready_time) * 1000).to_numpy()
    cnt = np.stack([rsg.counts(spikes, units, trs.ready_time.to_numpy() + t / 1000, -rsg.GLM_WINDOW_MS, 0,
                               rsg.GLM_WINDOW_MS)[:, 0, :] for t in ts_values], axis=1)
    rows, ys = [], []
    for i, (_, r) in enumerate(trs.iterrows()):
        for k, t in enumerate(ts_values):
            if elapsed[i] >= t - 1e-6:
                rows.append({"trial": i, "t": k, "prior": float(not r.is_short), "eff": float(not r.is_eye), "dir": float(r.theta == 180)})
                ys.append(cnt[i, k])
    return pd.DataFrame(rows), np.array(ys)


def design(df, with_t=True, with_prior=True):
    cols = [np.ones(len(df)), df.eff.to_numpy(), df["dir"].to_numpy()]
    if with_prior:
        cols.append(df.prior.to_numpy())
    if with_t:
        cols += [(df.t == k).to_numpy().astype(float) for k in range(1, 5)]
    return np.column_stack(cols)


def fit(y, X):
    r = sm.GLM(y, X, family=sm.families.Poisson()).fit()
    return r.llf, X.shape[1]


def bic(llf, k, n):
    return -2 * llf + k * np.log(n)


res = []
df_all, Y_all = glm_rows(good, rsg.SHORT_TS)
per_prior = {short: glm_rows(good[good.is_short == short], rsg.prior_ts(short)) for short in [True, False]}
for j, u in enumerate(units):
    y = Y_all[:, j]
    l_full, k_full = fit(y, design(df_all))
    l_red, k_red = fit(y, design(df_all, with_prior=False))
    n = len(y)
    row = {"unit": int(S["unit_ids"][u]), "prior_dBIC": bic(l_red, k_red, n) - bic(l_full, k_full, n),
           "prior_LR_p": stats.chi2.sf(2 * (l_full - l_red), k_full - k_red)}
    for short, (dfp, Yp) in per_prior.items():
        yp = Yp[:, j]
        lf, kf = fit(yp, design(dfp, with_prior=False))
        lr, kr = fit(yp, design(dfp, with_t=False, with_prior=False))
        row[f"ts_dBIC_{'short' if short else 'long'}"] = bic(lr, kr, len(yp)) - bic(lf, kf, len(yp))
        row[f"ts_LR_p_{'short' if short else 'long'}"] = stats.chi2.sf(2 * (lf - lr), kf - kr)
    res.append(row)
glm = pd.DataFrame(res)
glm["prior_dep"] = glm.prior_dBIC > 0
glm["ts_dep"] = (glm.ts_dBIC_short > 0) | (glm.ts_dBIC_long > 0)


def wilson(k, n):
    lo, hi = sm.stats.proportion_confint(k, n, method="wilson")
    return f"{100 * k / n:.1f}% ({k} of {n}; 95% interval {100 * lo:.1f} to {100 * hi:.1f}%)"


print("Rows (trial x time point): all trials", len(df_all), "; Short", len(per_prior[True][0]), "; Long", len(per_prior[False][0]))

print("ts-dependent (BIC):   ", wilson(int(glm.ts_dep.sum()), len(glm)), "; paper, H: 27%")
print("Both:", int((glm.prior_dep & glm.ts_dep).sum()), "; prior only:", int((glm.prior_dep & ~glm.ts_dep).sum()),

# Chance levels: the same BIC rule with the prior labels shuffled across trials within each
# effector and direction, and with the time points shuffled among the rows of each trial.
rng_glm = np.random.default_rng(7)
N_SHUFFLES = 5


def shuffled_prior(df, trs):
    lab = trs.is_short.to_numpy().copy()
    for _, idx in trs.reset_index(drop=True).groupby(["is_eye", "theta"]).groups.items():
        lab[idx] = rng_glm.permutation(lab[idx])
    out = df.copy()
    out["prior"] = (~lab[df.trial.to_numpy()]).astype(float)
    return out


def shuffled_time(df):
    out = df.copy()
    t = out.t.to_numpy().copy()
    for idx in out.groupby("trial").indices.values():
        t[idx] = rng_glm.permutation(t[idx])
    out["t"] = t
    return out


null_rows = []
for s in range(N_SHUFFLES):
    dfs = shuffled_prior(df_all, good)
    dft = {short: shuffled_time(dfp) for short, (dfp, _) in per_prior.items()}
    n_prior = n_ts_s = n_ts_l = n_ts = 0
    for j in range(len(units)):
        y = Y_all[:, j]
        lf, kf = fit(y, design(dfs))
        lr, kr = fit(y, design(dfs, with_prior=False))
        n_prior += bic(lr, kr, len(y)) - bic(lf, kf, len(y)) > 0
        dep = {}
        for short, (_, Yp) in per_prior.items():
            yp = Yp[:, j]
            lf, kf = fit(yp, design(dft[short], with_prior=False))
            lr, kr = fit(yp, design(dft[short], with_t=False, with_prior=False))
            dep[short] = bic(lr, kr, len(yp)) - bic(lf, kf, len(yp)) > 0
        n_ts_s += dep[True]
        n_ts_l += dep[False]
        n_ts += dep[True] or dep[False]
    null_rows.append({"shuffle": s, "prior_dep_pct": 100 * n_prior / len(units), "ts_dep_short_pct": 100 * n_ts_s / len(units),
                      "ts_dep_long_pct": 100 * n_ts_l / len(units), "ts_dep_either_pct": 100 * n_ts / len(units)})
glm_null = pd.DataFrame(null_rows)
print("Fractions of units passing the BIC rule with shuffled labels (%):")
print(glm_null.round(1).to_string(index=False))
print(f"\nObserved: prior {100 * glm.prior_dep.mean():.1f}%, ts in Short {100 * (glm.ts_dBIC_short > 0).mean():.1f}%, "
      f"ts in Long {100 * (glm.ts_dBIC_long > 0).mean():.1f}%, ts in either {100 * glm.ts_dep.mean():.1f}%")
print(f"Shuffled, maximum over {N_SHUFFLES}: prior {glm_null.prior_dep_pct.max():.1f}%, ts in either {glm_null.ts_dep_either_pct.max():.1f}%")

# Slow drift can mimic a prior effect when the priors come in blocks. Shift the prior labels
# along the session (as in the clock check) so that the block structure is kept.
print("\nPrior labels shifted along the session, block structure kept:")
for shift in [50, 100, 200]:
    lab = np.roll(good.is_short.to_numpy(), shift)
    dfs = df_all.copy()
    dfs["prior"] = (~lab[df_all.trial.to_numpy()]).astype(float)
    n_prior = 0
    for j in range(len(units)):
        y = Y_all[:, j]
        lf, kf = fit(y, design(dfs))
        lr, kr = fit(y, design(dfs, with_prior=False))
        n_prior += bic(lr, kr, len(y)) - bic(lf, kf, len(y)) > 0
    print(f"   shifted by {shift} trials: labels unchanged on {100 * (lab == good.is_short.to_numpy()).mean():.0f}% of trials; "
          f"prior-dependent {100 * n_prior / len(units):.1f}%")
runs = (good.is_short.to_numpy()[1:] != good.is_short.to_numpy()[:-1]).sum() + 1
print(f"Prior blocks in the session (runs of one prior over used trials): {runs}; median length "
      f"{np.median(np.diff(np.r_[0, np.flatnonzero(np.diff(good.is_short.to_numpy().astype(int))) + 1, len(good)])):.0f} trials")

Prior labels shifted along the session, block structure kept:

   shifted by 50 trials: labels unchanged on 56% of trials; prior-dependent 10.4%

   shifted by 100 trials: labels unchanged on 53% of trials; prior-dependent 14.6%

   shifted by 200 trials: labels unchanged on 48% of trials; prior-dependent 2.1%
Prior blocks in the session (runs of one prior over used trials): 87; median length 9 trials

Result: not reproduced. By the GLM and BIC rule of the Methods, 75.0% of units are prior-dependent (36 of 48, 95% interval 61.2 to 85.1%; paper 65 +/- 6.5%) and 45.8% are ts-dependent (22 of 48, interval 32.6 to 59.7%; paper 27 +/- 2.7%). Both fractions are above the paper's and outside tolerance; the interval of the prior fraction includes 65%, that of the ts fraction does not include 27%. With a likelihood-ratio test in place of BIC the fractions are higher still (prior 77.1 to 87.5%, ts 66.7 to 77.1%). The paper's fractions pool 536 units over 17 sessions; these 48 come from one session. Both fractions are far above chance. With the prior labels shuffled within effector and direction, 0 to 8.3% of units pass the prior test; with the labels shifted along the session by 50 to 200 trials, which keeps the blocks of the priors, 2.1 to 14.6%. With the time points shuffled within trials, 0 to 2.1% pass the ts test in either prior. Counting ts dependence in either prior's test gives 45.8%; the Short test alone gives 31.2% and the Long test alone 33.3%, both still above 27 +/- 2.7%.

dfr-overlap-support¶

At the overlapping ts of 800 ms, firing rates differ between priors, with the largest difference during the support of the prior, between 480 and 800 ms after Ready (Figure 3D).

In [15]:
rng_dfr = np.random.default_rng(3)
edges = np.arange(-320, 1440 + 1, 160)
centres = (edges[:-1] + edges[1:]) / 2


def rms_dfr(cnt, short):
    d = cnt[short].mean(0) - cnt[~short].mean(0)          # bins x units, counts per 160 ms
    return np.sqrt(np.mean((d * 1000 / 160) ** 2, axis=1))  # spikes/s

    cnts[name] = (rsg.counts(spikes, units, g.ready_time.to_numpy(), -320, 1440, 160), g.is_short.to_numpy())
    per_ds[name] = rms_dfr(*cnts[name])
mean_rms = np.mean(list(per_ds.values()), axis=0)
for _ in range(200):

# Stability of the peak: resample trials with replacement within each dataset and prior, and
# find the bin of the largest mean RMS difference.
rng_dfr_boot = np.random.default_rng(8)

for _ in range(200):
    per = []
    for cnt, lab in cnts.values():
        i = np.concatenate([rng_dfr_boot.choice(np.flatnonzero(lab == v), (lab == v).sum()) for v in (True, False)])
        per.append(rms_dfr(cnt[i], lab[i]))
    peaks.append(int(np.argmax(np.mean(per, axis=0))))
peaks = pd.Series(peaks).map(lambda k: f"{edges[k]} to {edges[k + 1]}")

480 to 640    192

Result: reproduced. At ts = 800 ms, the RMS over units of the Short minus Long rate difference, averaged over datasets, is largest in the bin 480 to 640 ms after Ready (6.86 spikes/s), within the support of the Short prior, and above the 95th percentile of the shuffled maximum (3.11). Before Ready it is at the shuffle level (2.39 and 2.29 against 95th percentiles of 2.42 and 2.32). Per dataset the largest bin is 480-640 (2 datasets), 640-800 and 800-960 ms; the mean is also high just after Set (6.07 in 800 to 960 ms). Over 200 bootstrap samples of trials the peak is in 480 to 640 ms in 192 and in 800 to 960 ms in 8, so it lies within 480 to 800 ms in 96% of samples.

Population trajectories¶

pca-dimensionality¶

Population activity is low dimensional; 3 to 4 principal components in the estimation epoch and 5 to 10 in the production epoch explain about 75% of the variance (Figure S3).

The PCA fitted here is used by the claims that follow.

In [18]:
EST, PROD, rows = {}, {}, []
for e, th, name in DS:
    g = good[(good.is_eye == e) & (good.theta == th)]
    est = {}
    for short in [True, False]:
        gg = g[g.is_short == short]
        rate, ends, n = rsg.estimation_rates(spikes, units, gg, max(rsg.prior_ts(short)))
        est[short] = {"rate": rate, "t": ends, "n": n}
    pca_e = rsg.PCA([est[True]["rate"], est[False]["rate"]])
    prod = {}
    for short in [True, False]:
        for ts in rsg.prior_ts(short):
            gg = g[(g.is_short == short) & (g.ts == ts)]
            prod[(short, ts)] = {"rate": rsg.production_rates(spikes, units, gg), "min_tp": gg.tp.min(),
                                 "mean_tp": gg.tp.mean(), "n": len(gg)}
    pca_p = rsg.PCA([v["rate"] for v in prod.values()])
    EST[name] = {"pca": pca_e, **est}
    PROD[name] = {"pca": pca_p, "traj": prod}
    cum_e, cum_p = np.cumsum(pca_e.explained), np.cumsum(pca_p.explained)
    rows.append({"dataset": name, "est_PCs_75": pca_e.n, "prod_PCs_75": pca_p.n,
                 "est_PCs_70": int(np.searchsorted(cum_e, .7) + 1), "est_PCs_80": int(np.searchsorted(cum_e, .8) + 1),
                 "prod_PCs_70": int(np.searchsorted(cum_p, .7) + 1), "prod_PCs_80": int(np.searchsorted(cum_p, .8) + 1),
                 "est_var_3PC": cum_e[2], "prod_var_5PC": cum_p[4]})

# Variants: rates normalised per unit before PCA (soft normalisation, and z-scoring), with the
# components reaching 75% of the variance. Estimation and production scales are taken from the
# trajectories that enter each PCA.
rows = []
for e, th, name in DS:
    E, P = EST[name], PROD[name]
    est_m = [E[True]["rate"], E[False]["rate"]]
    prod_m = [v["rate"] for v in P["traj"].values()]
    for how in ["soft", "z"]:
        se, sp = rsg.unit_scale(est_m, how), rsg.unit_scale(prod_m, how)
        pe = rsg.PCA([m / se for m in est_m])
        pp = rsg.PCA([m / sp for m in prod_m])
        E[f"pca_{how}"], E[f"scale_{how}"] = pe, se
        rows.append({"dataset": name, "normalisation": how, "est_PCs_75": pe.n, "prod_PCs_75": pp.n})

Result: not reproduced. Two components reach 75% of the variance in the estimation epoch in all 4 datasets (3 components explain 86 to 90%), and 2, 2, 5 and 4 in the production epoch, so 1 of the 8 values falls in the paper's ranges. Activity here is lower dimensional than the paper reports. This session has 48 units; the paper's PCA pools up to 536 units recorded over 17 sessions, which can add dimensions. The count depends on normalisation, which the Methods do not mention. With rates z-scored per unit, 3 or 4 components reach 75% in the estimation epoch and 6 to 10 in the production epoch, so all 8 values are in range; with soft normalisation (range plus 5 spikes/s) 6 of 8 are (production 4 in both eye datasets). The outcome is judged on unnormalised rates, as the claims file fixed before the analysis.

encoding-r2¶

Projections of estimation-epoch neural states onto the encoding axis match the Bayesian estimates from the model fitted to the behaviour (R2 = 0.993 for the Short prior, 0.996 for the Long prior, monkey H, Hand Left; Figure 4C).

In [20]:
rng_axes = np.random.default_rng(4)
PROJ, rows = {}, []
for e, th, name in DS:
    E = EST[name]
    for short in [True, False]:
        lo, hi = min(rsg.prior_ts(short)), max(rsg.prior_ts(short))
        X = E["pca"](E[short]["rate"])
        t = E[short]["t"]
        u = rsg.encoding_axis(X, t, lo, hi)
        sel = (t >= lo - 1e-6) & (t <= hi + 1e-6)
        xu, tt, w = X[sel] @ u, t[sel], E[short]["n"][sel]
        te = models[name].moments(tt, short)[0]
        _, _, r2_b, rmse_b = rsg.weighted_fit(te, xu, w)
        _, slope_ts, r2_l, rmse_l = rsg.weighted_fit(tt, xu, w)
        rand = []
        for _ in range(1000):
            v = rng_axes.standard_normal(X.shape[1])
            rand.append(rsg.weighted_fit(te, X[sel] @ (v / np.linalg.norm(v)), w)[2])
        rand = np.array(rand)
        PROJ[(name, short)] = {"t": tt, "xu": xu, "w": w, "te": te, "u": u, "X": X, "tall": t}
        rows.append({"dataset": name, "prior": "Short" if short else "Long", "points": int(sel.sum()), "PCs": X.shape[1],
                     "R2_bayes": r2_b, "RMSE_bayes": rmse_b, "R2_linear": r2_l, "RMSE_linear": rmse_l,
                     "slope_ts": slope_ts, "random_R2_median": np.median(rand),
                     "random_R2_95": np.percentile(rand, 95), "frac_random_above": np.mean(rand >= r2_b)})
enc = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(enc.round(4).to_string(index=False))

Result: reproduced. Under reading (a), Hand Left, R2 = 0.998 (Short) and 0.996 (Long); under reading (b), the mean of the 4 datasets, 0.959 and 0.989. Both readings are within tolerance. The estimation trajectories here have only 2 PCs, and projections on random unit vectors in that space also fit te well (median R2 0.73 to 0.98 by dataset and prior). The R2 on u exceeds that of 95% of random axes in 3 of 8 dataset-priors (Hand Right Long, both Hand Left priors), so in this session the fit is specific to u only for those three. With normalised rates (3 or 4 PCs) R2 stays above 0.94 in every dataset-prior (Hand Left 0.984 and 0.975 with soft normalisation, 0.990 and 0.960 z-scored), but the R2 on u exceeds that of 95% of random axes in 2 of 8 dataset-priors with soft normalisation and in 0 of 8 with z-scoring. The match to te is reproduced; its specificity to u is not shown in this session.

encoding-bayes-beats-linear¶

Neural projections are better explained by the Bayesian model than by a linear function of ts with the same number of parameters, for both priors (signed-rank test on RMSE, p = 0.008 for each prior; Figure 4D top).

In [24]:
# Variant: RMSE weighted by the number of trials in each bin, as in the fit.
def wrmse(x, y, w):
    a, b, _, _ = rsg.weighted_fit(x, y, w)
    return float(np.sqrt(np.sum(w * (y - a - b * x) ** 2) / np.sum(w)))


enc["dWRMSE"] = [wrmse(PROJ[(r.dataset, r.prior == "Short")]["te"], PROJ[(r.dataset, r.prior == "Short")]["xu"], PROJ[(r.dataset, r.prior == "Short")]["w"])
                 - wrmse(PROJ[(r.dataset, r.prior == "Short")]["t"], PROJ[(r.dataset, r.prior == "Short")]["xu"], PROJ[(r.dataset, r.prior == "Short")]["w"])
                 for r in enc.itertuples()]
for prior, g in enc.groupby("prior", sort=False):
    print(f"Weighted RMSE, {prior}: Bayesian lower in {(g.dWRMSE < 0).sum()} of 4; differences " + ", ".join(f"{x:+.3f}" for x in g.dWRMSE))

Weighted RMSE, Short: Bayesian lower in 3 of 4; differences -0.192, -0.424, +0.031, -0.052
Weighted RMSE, Long: Bayesian lower in 4 of 4; differences -0.204, -0.509, -0.103, -0.050

Result: partially reproduced. The Bayesian model has the lower RMSE in all 4 datasets for the Long prior and in 3 of 4 for the Short prior (Hand Right Short is the exception, 0.99 against 0.80). The differences are small: where the Bayesian model wins, it is better by 0.045 to 0.573 in units of Xu (spikes/s), and in Hand Right Short it is worse by 0.186. With the RMSE weighted by trial counts, as in the fit, the counts are the same (Long 4 of 4, Short 3 of 4, Hand Right Short +0.031). In the matched control period of the Long prior (short-in-long-control) the Bayesian model is also better in 3 of 4 datasets, so in this session its advantage is not specific to the support of the prior.

short-in-long-control¶

In the Long prior during the period matched to the support of the Short prior ("Short In Long"), the Bayesian model is not better than the linear one (signed-rank test, p = 0.74).

Result: reproduced by the paper's test, which cannot detect an effect here. The signed-rank test over the 4 datasets gives p = 0.25; with 4 datasets the smallest attainable p is 0.125, so it could not have found an effect. The effect sizes do not show the contrast the paper describes: in the control period the Bayesian model is better in 3 of 4 datasets, with a median relative RMSE difference of -0.089, at least as large as in the Short prior itself (-0.060).

neural-long-more-bias¶

Neural projections show more bias for the Long prior than for the Short prior, as a smaller regression slope of Xu on ts (signed-rank test, p = 0.008; Figure 4D bottom).

speed-vs-projection¶

# Both quantities depend on ts. Variant: residuals of each on ts (linear, within dataset and
# prior), pooled, so that only the variation not explained by ts is correlated.
def resid_on_ts(d, col):
    return d.groupby("dataset")[[col, "ts"]].apply(
        lambda h: pd.Series(h[col] - np.polyval(np.polyfit(h.ts, h[col], 1), h.ts), index=h.index)).droplevel(0)


for prior in ["Short", "Long"]:
    g = spd[spd.prior == prior]
    r, p = stats.pearsonr(resid_on_ts(g, "xu_at_set").loc[g.index], resid_on_ts(g, "speed").loc[g.index])
    print(f"{prior}: rho of residuals on ts = {r:.3f} (nominal p = {p:.2g}, not adjusted for the 8 fitted lines)")

Short: rho of residuals on ts = -0.195 (nominal p = 0.41, not adjusted for the 8 fitted lines)
Long: rho of residuals on ts = 0.069 (nominal p = 0.77, not adjusted for the 8 fitted lines)

Result: partially reproduced. Larger projections at Set are followed by slower production trajectories in both priors, more strongly than the paper reports: rho = -0.941 (Short, p = 6.2e-10) and -0.878 (Long, p = 3.7e-07), outside the tolerances around -0.74 and -0.51. Within each dataset the correlations are -0.75 to -1.00, and with Xu z-scored per dataset they are -0.759 and -0.779. Both quantities change with ts. With the residuals of each on ts within each dataset and prior, the correlation is -0.195 for Short and +0.069 for Long (nominal p = 0.41 and 0.77), so across conditions the relation is carried by their common dependence on ts. The paper's control for this, z-scoring within ts, applies to single-trial GPFA states of the production epoch, which are not computed here.

initial-speed-biased¶

The initial speed of production trajectories (Set to Set + 400 ms) is biased toward the middle of the prior; its dependence on ts is shallower than the unbiased profile proportional to 1/ts (signed-rank test, p < 1e-3 over conditions and animals; Figure 4F).

In [29]:
rows, dropped = [], 0
for e, th, name in DS:
    g = good[(good.is_eye == e) & (good.theta == th)]
    for short in [True, False]:
        ts_v = np.array(rsg.prior_ts(short), float)
        sp = []
        for ts in ts_v:
            gg = g[(g.is_short == short) & (g.ts == ts)]
            dropped += int((gg.tp < 400).sum())
            gg = gg[gg.tp >= 400]
            sp.append(rsg.step_speed(PROD[name]["pca"](rsg.production_rates(spikes, units, gg, 400))))
        sp = np.array(sp)
        unbiased = sp[2] * ts_v[2] / ts_v
        rows.append({"dataset": name, "prior": "Short" if short else "Long", **{f"speed_{int(t)}": s for t, s in zip(ts_v, sp)},
                     "slope_measured": np.polyfit(ts_v, sp, 1)[0], "slope_unbiased": np.polyfit(ts_v, unbiased, 1)[0]})

ini["measured_minus_unbiased"] = ini.slope_measured - ini.slope_unbiased

      f"two-sided signed-rank p = {w.pvalue:.4f}; trials dropped for tp < 400 ms: {dropped}")
print("Measured slope negative in", int((ini.slope_measured < 0).sum()), "of 8")

speed-predicts-tp¶

The speed of neural trajectories in the production epoch predicts the mean tp (Pearson correlation, rho Short = -0.58, rho Long = -0.52; Figure 4G).

# z-scored within each dataset, prior and ts, then correlated.

for col in ["speed", "tp"]:
    tt_[f"z_{col}"] = tt_.groupby(["dataset", "prior", "ts"])[col].transform(lambda x: (x - x.mean()) / x.std())
zr = tt_.groupby(["dataset", "prior"], sort=False).apply(lambda h: pd.Series(stats.pearsonr(h.z_speed, h.z_tp), index=["r", "p"]))

for prior, g in tt_.groupby("prior", sort=False):
    r, p = stats.pearsonr(g.z_speed, g.z_tp)
    print(f"{prior}, pooled over datasets: r = {r:.3f} (p = {p:.2g}, {len(g)} trials); negative in "
          f"{int((zr.loc[(slice(None), prior), 'r'] < 0).sum())} of 4, p < 0.05 and negative in "
          f"{int(((zr.loc[(slice(None), prior), 'r'] < 0) & (zr.loc[(slice(None), prior), 'p'] < 0.05)).sum())}")

# Null for the trial-by-trial measure: units fire as Poisson processes at a constant rate (each
# unit's mean from Set to Go in the dataset and prior), each trial keeps its own duration tp, and
# speed is measured as above. Shorter trials average fewer bins, which alone could tie speed to tp.
rng_tt = np.random.default_rng(11)
null_r = {"Short": [], "Long": []}
for _ in range(20):
    sims = []
    for e, th, name in DS:
        g = good[(good.is_eye == e) & (good.theta == th)]
        for short in [True, False]:
            gg = g[g.is_short == short]
            nbs = (gg.tp.to_numpy() // rsg.BIN_MS).astype(int)
            c_ = rsg.counts(spikes, units, gg.set_time.to_numpy(), 0, 2400)
            lam = np.concatenate([c_[i, :n] for i, n in enumerate(nbs)]).mean(0)
            for ts, tp, n in zip(gg.ts, gg.tp, nbs):
                sim = rng_tt.poisson(lam, size=(n, len(units))).astype(float)
                sims.append({"dataset": name, "prior": "Short" if short else "Long", "ts": ts, "tp": tp,
                             "speed": rsg.step_speed(PROD[name]["pca"](rsg.smooth(sim * 1000 / rsg.BIN_MS)))})
    sims = pd.DataFrame(sims)
    for col in ["speed", "tp"]:
        sims[f"z_{col}"] = sims.groupby(["dataset", "prior", "ts"])[col].transform(lambda x: (x - x.mean()) / x.std())
    for prior, g in sims.groupby("prior"):
        null_r[prior].append(stats.pearsonr(g.z_speed, g.z_tp)[0])
for prior in ["Short", "Long"]:
    g = tt_[tt_.prior == prior]
    r = stats.pearsonr(g.z_speed, g.z_tp)[0]
    v = np.array(null_r[prior])
    print(f"Poisson null with matched durations, {prior}: null r mean {v.mean():.3f}, range {v.min():.3f} to {v.max():.3f} "
          f"(20 simulations); observed {r:.3f}, below every null value: {bool(r < v.min())}")

Xu -45.0 to 24.2; speed 3.15 to 9.13; mean tp 497 to 1177; all within the axes.

Result: partially reproduced. Faster production trajectories go with shorter mean tp in both priors: rho = -0.733 (Short, p = 0.00024) and -0.744 (Long, p = 0.00017) over 20 points, stronger than the paper's -0.58 and -0.52 and outside tolerance. Within datasets the correlations are -0.80 to -0.99. The benchmark's trial-by-trial variant gives r = -0.195 to -0.740 (mean -0.519), with 7 of 8 conditions at p < 0.05. With the residuals on ts within each dataset and prior the correlation is +0.084 (Short) and -0.283 (Long), nominal p = 0.72 and 0.23. Trial by trial, with speed and tp z-scored within each ts as in the paper's control, faster trials go with shorter tp: r = -0.317 (Short, 481 trials, p = 1.1e-12) and -0.201 (Long, 502 trials, p = 5.5e-06), negative in all 8 dataset-priors and with p < 0.05 in 6 (4 Short, 2 Long). Shorter trials have fewer bins to average noise over, which could by itself tie speed to tp. For Poisson units at constant rates, with each trial's own duration, the same measure gives null r of -0.071 (Short) and -0.033 (Long) on average over 20 simulations, and the observed values are below every null value (null ranges -0.144 to -0.010 and -0.103 to +0.028). The duration accounts for a small part of the trial-by-trial correlation.

Alternative mechanisms¶

alt-speed-unmodulated¶

Instantaneous speed of neural trajectories in the full neural space is not modulated during the support of each prior (signed-rank test for zero regression slopes, p = 0.64 for Short, p = 0.08 for Long; Figure 5B).

In [33]:
rng_boot = np.random.default_rng(5)


def support_slope(rate, ends, short):
    lo, hi = min(rsg.prior_ts(short)), max(rsg.prior_ts(short))
    sp = np.linalg.norm(np.diff(rate, axis=0), axis=1)
    t = ends[1:]
    sel = (t > lo) & (t <= hi + 1e-6)
    return np.polyfit(t[sel], sp[sel], 1)[0] * 100, sp[sel].mean()   # per 100 ms

        c_ = rsg.counts(spikes, units, gg.ready_time.to_numpy(), 0, t_max)

# Attrition adds noise: later bins average fewer trials, and noisier rates give larger steps.
# Variant 1: only the trials with the longest ts of the prior, which last the whole support, so
# the number of trials is the same in every bin. Null: units firing as Poisson processes at a
# constant rate (each unit's mean over the support before Set), with the same trials and
# Set times, measured both ways. The point estimate of the main measure is also compared with
# the median of its bootstrap.
rng_null = np.random.default_rng(10)
rows = []
for e, th, name in DS:
    g = good[(good.is_eye == e) & (good.theta == th)]
    for short in [True, False]:
        gg = g[g.is_short == short]
        lo, hi = min(rsg.prior_ts(short)), max(rsg.prior_ts(short))
        c_ = rsg.counts(spikes, units, gg.ready_time.to_numpy(), 0, hi)
        el = ((gg.set_time - gg.ready_time) * 1000).to_numpy()
        ends = np.arange(1, c_.shape[1] + 1) * rsg.BIN_MS
        full = gg.ts.to_numpy() == hi
        fixed = support_slope(rsg.smooth(c_[full].mean(0) * 1000 / rsg.BIN_MS), ends, short)[0]
        use = (el[:, None] >= ends[None, :] - 1e-6) & (ends[None, :] > lo)
        lam = c_[use].mean(0)                          # counts per bin and unit, before Set, in the support
        null_main, null_fixed, null_speed = [], [], []
        for _ in range(100):
            sim = rng_null.poisson(lam, size=c_.shape).astype(float)
            sl_, sp_ = support_slope(rsg.attrition_rates(sim, el)[0], ends, short)
            null_main.append(sl_)
            null_speed.append(sp_)
            null_fixed.append(support_slope(rsg.smooth(sim[full].mean(0) * 1000 / rsg.BIN_MS), ends, short)[0])
        main = asp[(asp.dataset == name) & (asp.prior == ("Short" if short else "Long"))].iloc[0]
        rows.append({"dataset": name, "prior": "Short" if short else "Long", "speed_obs": main.mean_speed,
                     "speed_null_mean": np.mean(null_speed), "slope_main": main.slope_per_100ms,
                     "null_main_mean": np.mean(null_main), "null_main_95": np.percentile(null_main, 95),
                     "trials_full": int(full.sum()), "slope_fixed": fixed, "null_fixed_mean": np.mean(null_fixed),
                     "null_fixed_2.5": np.percentile(null_fixed, 2.5), "null_fixed_97.5": np.percentile(null_fixed, 97.5)})
spn = pd.DataFrame(rows)
spn["excess_main"] = spn.slope_main - spn.null_main_mean
print("Slopes of speed per 100 ms of the support; Poisson null of constant rates, 100 simulations:")
print(spn.round(3).to_string(index=False))
for prior, g in spn.groupby("prior", sort=False):
    print(f"{prior}: main slope above the null's 95th percentile in {(g.slope_main > g.null_main_95).sum()} of 4; "

          f"positive in {(g.slope_fixed > 0).sum()} of 4; signed-rank p (fixed trials) = {stats.wilcoxon(g.slope_fixed).pvalue:.3f}")
print(f"\nMean speed over the support: null above observed in {(spn.speed_null_mean > spn.speed_obs).sum()} of 8 "
      f"(null / observed {(spn.speed_null_mean / spn.speed_obs).min():.2f} to {(spn.speed_null_mean / spn.speed_obs).max():.2f})")
print("\nBootstrap of the main measure: point estimate below the bootstrap 2.5th percentile in",
      int((asp.slope_per_100ms < asp.boot_low).sum()), "of 8, so the bootstrap is biased upward and its intervals are not used.")

Result: reproduced by the paper's test, which cannot detect an effect here. The signed-rank test over 4 datasets gives p = 0.125 for each prior, the smallest value it can give, so the outcome carries no evidence for the absence of modulation. All 8 slopes of speed on time are positive, but noise alone produces positive slopes of this size: later bins average fewer trials, and noisier rates give larger steps. For units firing as Poisson processes at constant rates, with the same trials and Set times, the mean null slope is above the observed slope in all 8 dataset-priors, and no observed slope exceeds the null's 95th percentile. With only the trials of the longest ts, which last the whole support, the slopes are -0.106 to +0.529 per 100 ms and fall outside the null's 95% range in 1 of 8 (Hand Right Long, below it). The bootstrap intervals over trials are biased upward (the point estimate is below the interval in 2 of 8) and are not used. The observed slopes are below the null mean in all 8 dataset-priors, with all trials and with fixed trials. The null is not noisier than the data overall: its mean speed over the support is below the observed one in 7 of 8 (null / observed 0.65 to 1.18). The observed speed thus rises less over the support than noise alone would make it rise, which points to a speed that falls during the support, as long as the units' noise is no larger than Poisson. This was not tested further. The data show no speed increase beyond what noise produces, and the paper's test has no power to show a change in either direction.

alt-transient-parallel¶

In the first 200 ms after Set, trajectories for different ts run parallel; their distance to the middle ts trajectory does not change (signed-rank test for zero slopes, p = 0.92 for the shortest ts, p = 0.13 for the longest; Figure 5D).

In [35]:
def transient_slopes(kept=rsg.VAR_KEPT, norm=None):
    rows = []
    for e, th, name in DS:
        g = good[(good.is_eye == e) & (good.theta == th)]
        traj = {}
        for short in [True, False]:
            for ts in rsg.prior_ts(short):
                gg = g[(g.is_short == short) & (g.ts == ts)]
                traj[(short, ts)] = rsg.aligned_rates(spikes, units, gg.set_time.to_numpy(), -100, 300)[5:15]  # Set to Set + 200 ms
        if norm:
            sc = rsg.unit_scale(list(traj.values()), norm)
            traj = {k: v / sc for k, v in traj.items()}
        pca_t = rsg.PCA(list(traj.values()), kept) if kept else (lambda x: x)
        t = np.arange(1, 11) * rsg.BIN_MS
        for short in [True, False]:
            ts_v = rsg.prior_ts(short)
            ref = pca_t(traj[(short, ts_v[2])])
            for which, ts in [("shortest", ts_v[0]), ("longest", ts_v[-1])]:
                dist = np.linalg.norm(pca_t(traj[(short, ts)]) - ref, axis=1)
                rows.append({"dataset": name, "prior": "Short" if short else "Long", "ts": which,
                             "PCs": getattr(pca_t, "n", len(units)), "mean_distance": dist.mean(),
                             "slope_per_100ms": np.polyfit(t, dist, 1)[0] * 100})
    out = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    out["slope_rel_pct"] = 100 * out.slope_per_100ms / out.mean_distance
    return out

    w = stats.wilcoxon(g.slope_per_100ms)

          f"median relative slope {g.slope_rel_pct.median():+.1f}% per 100 ms")
print("\nVariants (signed-rank p for the shortest and the longest ts; PCs kept per dataset):")
for kept, norm, lab in [(0.60, None, "60% of variance"), (0.90, None, "90% of variance"), (None, None, "full space"),
                        (0.75, "z", "z-scored rates, 75%"), (0.75, "soft", "soft-normalised rates, 75%")]:
    v = transient_slopes(kept, norm)
    ps = {w: stats.wilcoxon(g.slope_per_100ms).pvalue for w, g in v.groupby("ts")}
    pos = {w: int((g.slope_per_100ms > 0).sum()) for w, g in v.groupby("ts")}
    print(f"   {lab}: shortest p = {ps['shortest']:.3f} ({pos['shortest']} of 8 positive), longest p = {ps['longest']:.3f} "
          f"({pos['longest']} of 8 positive); PCs {v.groupby('dataset', sort=False).PCs.first().tolist()}")

For the longest ts, the distance to the middle trajectory changes in the first 200 ms after Set: 6 of 8 slopes are negative (median -15.3% of the mean distance per 100 ms), signed-rank p = 0.039. For the shortest ts p = 0.078 (6 of 8 positive, median +26.7% per 100 ms). The PCA kept 1 to 4 components, and in Eye Left a single component, where the distance is the absolute difference along one axis. The result holds for the longest ts with other numbers of components: p = 0.016 with 60% of the variance, 0.039 with 90%, 0.023 in the full space of 48 units and 0.039 with z-scored rates (75%); with soft-normalised rates it is 0.055. For the shortest ts p is 0.078 to 0.742 across these variants.

alt-threshold-monotonic¶

Aligned to the response, distances between trajectories for different ts decrease steadily up to movement initiation, without the converging then diverging pattern a ts-dependent threshold would produce (Figure 5F).

def go_curves(kept, min_n=1):
    rows, curves = [], {}
    for e, th, name in DS:
        g = good[(good.is_eye == e) & (good.theta == th)]
        traj = {}
        for short in [True, False]:
            for ts in rsg.prior_ts(short):
                gg = g[(g.is_short == short) & (g.ts == ts)]
                traj[(short, ts)] = rsg.aligned_rates(spikes, units, gg.go_time.to_numpy(), -900, 100)[5:45]  # Go - 800 to Go
        pca_g = rsg.PCA(list(traj.values()), kept, min_n) if kept else (lambda x: x)
        t = np.arange(-39, 1) * rsg.BIN_MS   # bin end times relative to Go
        for short in [True, False]:
            ts_v = rsg.prior_ts(short)
            ref = pca_g(traj[(short, ts_v[2])])
            for ts in ts_v[:2] + ts_v[3:]:
                diff = pca_g(traj[(short, ts)]) - ref
                dist = np.linalg.norm(diff, axis=1)
                curves[(name, short, ts)] = dist
                k = np.argmin(dist)
                # With one component, a minimum is a crossing when the signed difference changes sign there.
                crossing = diff.shape[1] == 1 and np.any(np.sign(diff[max(k - 1, 0):k + 2, 0]) != np.sign(diff[k, 0]))
                rows.append({"dataset": name, "prior": "Short" if short else "Long", "ts": ts,
                             "PCs": getattr(pca_g, "n", len(units)), "t_min": t[np.argmin(dist)],
                             "d_at_go_over_min": dist[-1] / dist.min(), "min_at_crossing": bool(crossing), "d_start": dist[0], "d_go": dist[-1]})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows), curves, t

      f"minimum in the last 40 ms in {(thr_tab.t_min >= -20).sum()} of {len(thr_tab)} curves; in the last 200 ms in "
      f"{(thr_tab.t_min >= -180).sum()}; distance at Go below that 800 ms earlier in {(thr_tab.d_go < thr_tab.d_start).sum()}")
for kept, lab in [(0.75, "75% of variance"), (None, "full space")]:

Result: not reproduced. With the components that reach 60% of the variance (1 to 3 per dataset), the median time of the minimum distance is 210 ms before Go; the minimum is in the last 40 ms in 6 of 32 curves and in the last 200 ms in 14. The distance at Go is below that 800 ms earlier in 26 of 32 curves, so distances do fall overall. The result depends on the number of components: with 75% of the variance the median minimum is 80 ms before Go, and in the full space of 48 units 40 ms before Go, which would meet the criterion. With 1 component (Eye datasets) the distance can reach zero where trajectories cross, which moves the minima. In the eye datasets, with 1 component (16 curves), the signed difference changes sign at the minimum in 12 curves, so these minima are crossings; in 4 curves the minimum is at Go (3 of them not crossings), and the distance at Go is more than 10 times the minimum in 5. Requiring at least 2 components gives a median minimum 230 ms before Go, and at least 3 gives 70 ms before Go, within the 200 ms of a partial reproduction. The outcome is judged on the criterion's 60% of the variance.

Single-trial trajectories (GPFA)¶

gpfa-variance-inverted-u¶

The variance across single trials of the GPFA neural state at Set projected on the encoding axis has an inverted-U profile over ts, lower at the extremes of each prior (one-tailed signed-rank test on quadratic coefficients, p = 0.0273, monkey H; Figure 6C).

In [39]:
rng_gpfa = np.random.default_rng(6)
t_gpfa = time.time()


def gpfa_rows(name, g, lat):
    rows = []
    for short in [True, False]:
        mask = g.is_short.to_numpy() == short
        L = [lat[i] for i in np.flatnonzero(mask)]
        nb = max(x.shape[1] for x in L)
        mean = np.array([np.mean([x[:, k] for x in L if x.shape[1] > k], axis=0) for k in range(nb)])
        tt = np.arange(1, nb + 1) * rsg.BIN_MS
        ts_v = rsg.prior_ts(short)
        u = rsg.encoding_axis(mean, tt, min(ts_v), max(ts_v))
        xu = np.array([x[:, -1] @ u for x in L])
        ts_tr = g.ts.to_numpy()[mask]
        z = (xu - xu.mean()) / xu.std()
        var = np.array([z[ts_tr == t].var(ddof=1) for t in ts_v])
        mxu = np.array([xu[ts_tr == t].mean() for t in ts_v])
        rows.append({"dataset": name, "prior": "Short" if short else "Long", **{f"var_{t}": v for t, v in zip(ts_v, var)},
                     "quad_coef": np.polyfit(np.array(ts_v, float), var, 2)[0],
                     "mean_xu": mxu, "slope_xu": np.polyfit(np.array(ts_v, float), mxu, 1)[0]})
    return rows


GP, rows = {}, []
for e, th, name in DS:
    g = good[(good.is_eye == e) & (good.theta == th)]
    sts = rsg.estimation_spiketrains(spikes, units, g)
    model, dim, scores, folds = rsg.fit_gpfa(sts, rng_gpfa)
    lat = rsg.gpfa_transform(model, sts)
    GP[name] = {"lat": lat, "trials": g, "dim": dim, "sts": sts, "folds": folds, "scores": scores, "model": model}
    print(f"{name}: {len(g)} trials, latent dimensionality {dim} (cross-validated log-likelihood "
          + ", ".join(f"{k}: {v:.0f}" for k, v in scores.items()) + ")")
    rows += gpfa_rows(name, g, lat)
gp = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(f"GPFA fits took {time.time() - t_gpfa:.0f} s")

# Convergence: the training log-likelihood of each final model over its EM iterations
# (computed every fifth iteration), and the relative gain over the last 25 iterations.
print("Training log-likelihood of the final models:")
for name, G in GP.items():
    ll = np.array(G["model"].fit_info["log_likelihoods"], float)
    it = np.flatnonzero(~np.isnan(ll)) + 1
    ll = ll[~np.isnan(ll)]
    late = ll[it >= it[-1] - 25][0]
    print(f"   {name}: {len(G['model'].fit_info['log_likelihoods'])} iterations; at iteration 50 {ll[it == 50][0]:.0f}, "
          f"75 {ll[it == 75][0]:.0f}, {it[-1]} {ll[-1]:.0f}; gain over the last 25 iterations {100 * (ll[-1] - late) / abs(ll[-1]):.3f}%")

# Variant: a wider grid; 12 latents scored on the same folds. Where 12 wins, the variance test
# is repeated with the 12-latent model.
t_var = time.time()
rows_12, wins = [], []
for name, G in GP.items():
    s12 = rsg.gpfa_cv_score(G["sts"], G["folds"], 12)
    best = max({**G["scores"], 12: s12}.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1])[0]
    print(f"{name}: cross-validated log-likelihood with 12 latents {s12:.0f} (chosen {G['dim']}: {G['scores'][G['dim']]:.0f}); best of 4, 8, 12: {best}")
    if best == 12:
        wins.append(name)
        lat12 = rsg.gpfa_transform(rsg.gpfa_model(G["sts"], 12), G["sts"])
        rows_12 += gpfa_rows(name, G["trials"], lat12)
    else:
        rows_12 += [r.to_dict() for _, r in gp[gp.dataset == name].iterrows()]
gp12 = pd.DataFrame(rows_12)
w12 = stats.wilcoxon(gp12.quad_coef, alternative="less")
print(f"With the grid 4, 8, 12 ({len(wins)} datasets refit with 12): quadratic coefficient negative in "
      f"{(gp12.quad_coef < 0).sum()} of 8; one-tailed signed-rank p = {w12.pvalue:.4f}")
inc12 = np.array([np.subtract(*rsg.increments(m)[::-1]) for m in gp12.mean_xu])
sg12 = gp12.pivot(index="dataset", columns="prior", values="slope_xu")
print(f"Mean projections with this grid: middle increment above extreme in {(inc12 > 0).sum()} of 8 "
      f"(two-sided p = {stats.wilcoxon(inc12).pvalue:.4f}); Short slope above Long in {int((sg12.Short > sg12.Long).sum())} of 4")
print(f"Variant took {time.time() - t_var:.0f} s")

Result: not reproduced. The quadratic coefficient of variance on ts is negative in 5 of 8 dataset-priors; the one-tailed signed-rank test gives p = 0.125 (paper 0.0273). Cross-validation chose 8 latent dimensions in all 4 datasets, the larger of the two candidates. Cross-validation does not settle the dimensionality: 12 latents, scored on the same folds as a variant, beat 8 in all 4 datasets. With 12 latents the quadratic coefficient is negative in 5 of 8 and p = 0.125, the same result. After 100 EM iterations the training log-likelihood was still rising, by less than 0.1% over the last 25 iterations (0.064 to 0.085% in this run), so the fits are close to convergence but not at it.

gpfa-mean-sigmoid¶

The mean of the single-trial GPFA projections is sigmoidal (signed-rank test on increments, p = 0.0078) and has a higher slope for the Short prior (one-tailed signed-rank, p = 0.0625; Figure 6D).

Result: reproduced. The mean single-trial projection rises with ts in all 8 dataset-priors, its middle increments exceed those at the extremes in 8 of 8 (two-sided signed-rank p = 0.0078, the paper's value), and its slope is higher for the Short prior in 4 of 4 datasets (one-tailed p = 0.0625, the paper's value). With 12 latents the middle increments exceed the extreme ones in 8 of 8 (p = 0.0078) and the Short slope is higher in 4 of 4.

Summary¶

A failure to reproduce here may be a failure of this attempt, not of the paper: see the reasoning and the differences from the paper's method.

How the analysis differs from the paper's. All results come from one session of monkey H, one of the 29 sessions of the paper, with 48 units where the paper analyses 536 (H) and 636 (G) units, of 617 and 741 recorded, over sessions; a "dataset" here is one effector and direction in this session (4, against the paper's 8). The paper's code was not available, so smoothing, the encoding axis, speed, the GLM design with attrition and the Bayesian observer fit follow the Methods as read and the choices stated in the claims file. The paper's signed-rank tests over 8 datasets become tests over 4, which cannot reach p < 0.05; two claims of absence are judged on such tests. The GPFA latent dimensionality was chosen from 4 and 8 only, with 100 EM iterations; 12 latents score better, and the conclusions do not change with them. The outlier flag is the file's. Rates are not normalised before PCA, as the Methods do not say; z-scoring them brings the PCA dimensionality into the paper's ranges; the encoding axis then still scores above the median random axis in all 8 dataset-priors, but above 95% of random axes in none.

What was found about the dandiset. It holds one session of one of the paper's two monkeys, in the form prepared for the Neural Latents Benchmark: 283 of the session's trials are in a test file without task variables and without 14 of the 54 units. The 48 units that pass the Methods' rate rule match the paper's single-session GPFA count for monkey H, consistent with this being that session. The iti description gives the priors' inter-trial intervals the wrong way round, tp is a median 18 ms longer than go_time - set_time, the is_outlier flag is not reproduced by a refit of the Methods' mixture model (10 of 46 flagged), and units have no single-unit or multi-unit label and no electrode, whose table has no positions.
